profile.summary: Obadiah is a brief prophecy of judgment against Edom, neighbor and relative of Judah, for his posture of pride, hostility, and complicity in the fall of Jerusalem before Babylon. The book shows that God does not ignore violence or fraternal betrayal: what Edom did to Judah would return upon Edom according to divine justice. At the same time, prophecy announces the restoration of the oppressed people and points to the Lord's Day, when God's rule will manifest itself in full over the nations.
profile.setting: The backdrop is the crisis of Judah in 586 BC, when Jerusalem was destroyed by Babylon and the kingdom fell. Edom, descended from Esau and traditional neighboring southeast of Judah, occupied mountainous regions east of the Arabah and south of the Dead Sea. Although his history with Israel was long and marked by tensions, the most serious offense highlighted here is his reaction to the ruin of Jerusalem: instead of solidarity, Edom rejoiced and collaborated with the invaders. As for the date and authorship, the book is attributed to Obadiah, but it is a little known figure; the most likely date, according to the introduction, is soon after the destruction of Jerusalem, although the text does not completely eliminate the debate.

structure.label: Judgment against Edom and hope for Zion
structure.description: The single chapter moves from the denunciation of Edom's pride and humiliation to the affirmation of the Lord's Day, in which the oppressors will be judged and Judah will be restored, culminating in the vision of the universal kingdom of the Lord.

themes: Retributive justice of God in the face of violence
Responsibility in the face of the suffering of others
Judgment of the nations and the Lord's Day
Restoration of Judah and the universal reign of God
readingKeys: Notice the contrast between Edom and Judah: whoever rejoices at the fall of the other ends also under judgment.
Read the book as a unity: denunciation of sin, proclamation of judgment, and promise of restoration go together.
Pay attention to the images of height, security and ruin, which underline the pride of Edom and its reversal.
Note that the local prophecy about Edom also opens to a broader horizon, involving all nations and the reign of the Lord.
profile.cautions: The introduction associates Obadiah with the context of the fall of Jerusalem and says that the most likely date is soon after 586 BC, but recognizes that the prophet is little identified and that the exact date is absolutely not certain. Moreover, some literary relations with other prophets are suggested, not definitively proven. In reading, avoid reducing the book to mere national revenge: it deals with divine justice, moral responsibility and restoration of the oppressed people.

dossier.narratedEra: The scenario narrated in Obadiah is the crisis of Jerusalem in the face of the Babylonian invasion and its immediate consequences for Judah and Edom. The background includes historical animosity between Edom/Esau and Israel/Jacob, the fall of Jerusalem, the plundering of the city, and the advance of a divine judgment on the nations (especially Edom).
dossier.compositionEra: The sources suggest a composition shortly after the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC, although Matthew Henry records that some think of an older, contemporary date from Hosea, Joel and Amos. Tyndale considers it likely that Obadiah wrote shortly after the fall of Jerusalem, with the text responding directly to the Babylonian invasion.

politics.title: Edom as a ravage nation and rival of Judah
politics.detail: Edom existed for much of the monarchy of Israel, and was often vassal of the southern kingdom, Judah. The note also recalls that Edom occupied the highlands east of the Arabah and the south of the Dead Sea.
politics.readingImpact: This makes Edom a politically dependent neighbor, but also fraternally responsible. The prophecy does not deal with a distant enemy, but of an ally/parent that broke duties of loyalty.

politics.title: Edom's Conlution with Babylon against Jerusalem
politics.detail: The notes say that when Jerusalem was destroyed, Edom not only rejoiced, but also aligned himself with the Babylonians and took part in the plunder; Tyndale observes that Edom made a covenant with Babylon rather than his brother Israel.
politics.readingImpact: The reading of Obadias gains the tone of judicial process: Edom's sin is not only omission, but betrayal in the context of war and national collapse.

politics.title: Nebuchadnezzar and the fall of Judah
politics.detail: The introduction is in the crisis in 586 BC, when the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar ended the independence of Judah and exiled Zedekiah.
politics.readingImpact: The book should be read as a prophetic reaction to a concrete historical event, not as a generic threat. This explains why Edom's attack is so morally serious in the notes.

politics.title: Dispute between coalitions and political retribution
politics.detail: Tyndale highlights the image of an "embassy" calling the nations to unite against Edom, typical language of military coalition. Then, ironically, these same forces or nations also enter the horizon of divine judgment.
politics.readingImpact: The reader realizes that divine sovereignty overlaps human alliances: Edom's political covenants and military coalitions do not protect him from judgment.

politics.title: Babylonian Empire as Historical Agent of Judgment
politics.detail: The notes identify the Babylonians as destroyers of Jerusalem and associate Edom's response to this context; Matthew Henry also speaks of the "destruction of Jerusalem" as the backdrop of the book.
politics.readingImpact: Babylon is not only a scenario, but a historical instrument by which the drama between Judah and Edom becomes visible, which reinforces the language of retribution in Obadiah.

politics.title: Restoration of Judah and subjugation of Edom
politics.detail: The final section is read as a promise of reversal: Judah will be restored and Edom will be subdued as an example of the fate of those who oppose the government of the Lord.
politics.readingImpact: The book does not end in the suffering of Judah, but in the political reversal of the situation: the oppressed people recover place and territory under the divine reign.

customs.title: Hospitality and fraternal responsibility violated
customs.detail: The notes deal with the relationship between Edom and Israel as fraternal, demanding duties of solidarity. Edom was supposed to have been allaado of Brother Israel, but he chose treason.
customs.readingImpact: The text is also read as an ethical denunciation of a breakdown of family and neighborhood duty, not only as a conflict between states.

customs.title: War de lack and sharing of spoil
customs.detail: Tyndale notes that Edom took part in the spoil of Jerusalem. The note on thieves and reapers also suggests the contrast between looting and normal collection practices, with limits of survival and care for the poor.
customs.readingImpact: The plunder is presented as a concrete moral violation; the reader understands that Edom went beyond the common opportunism in war and exceeded the minimum limits recognized by the law.

customs.title: Escape, repatriation and violence against refugees
customs.detail: The notes claim that Edom participated in arresting, killing or repatriating fugitives from Judah. Language assumes flows of refugees after the fall of the city.
customs.readingImpact: Obadias denounces not only war between armies, but also violence against vulnerable people in displacement, extending the ethical gravity of the accusation.

customs.title: Life in mountain fortresses
customs.detail: Edom relied on his rocky topography and fortresses in high places. The image of the "falesias" and physical security appears as a trace of his collective self-confidence.
customs.readingImpact: Geography becomes a symbol of illusory security: the reader realizes that defensive position and defense engineering do not prevent the fall before the divine judgment.

customs.title: Loot economy and accumulated wealth
customs.detail: Matthew Henry summarizes the threats against Edom in terms of looted wealth; Tyndale details that Edom hoped to gain material advantage from the fall of Jerusalem.
customs.readingImpact: The book's economy is of retribution: gains made by war opportunism will be reversed, and this shapes the reading of 1:5-7 as a critique of war greed.

customs.title: People remaining and resettlement in Judah
customs.detail: Tyndale mentions a remnant of Judah in Jerusalem and describes regions such as Neguebe, Philistine Plains, Gilead, Ephraim and Samaria as areas of resettlement and expansion. This involves post-exile everyday life, return and territorial occupation.
customs.readingImpact: Promised restoration is not abstract: it involves real return to territory, community survival and recomposition of national life under divine blessing.

language.title: "Vision as prophetic formula
language.detail: The note of Obadiah 1:1 explains that ""vision" introduces a prophetic book and designates something really seen/perceived as a divine word. False views are distinguished by not being fulfilled.
language.readingImpact: This guides the reading of Obadiah as a revelation validated by historical fulfillment, not as mere religious rhetoric.

language.title: Legal image and accusation of crack break
language.detail: In 1:10-14, Tyndale speaks of "legal terms" and in evidence that supports the accusation of breaking the covenant. Matthew Henry also organizes the book in threats and promises, as a forensic play.
language.readingImpact: The reader should listen to the text as a divine judicial process, in which Edom is called to respond for crime against his brother.

language.title: Irony of pride and topographic safety
language.detail: The 1:2-4 note connects Edom's pride to the mountainous relief that gave him safety. The high of the fortress symbolizes the high of its superb.
language.readingImpact: Language transforms geography into a moral metaphor: the higher the self-image of Edom, the more dramatic his humiliation.

language.title: The Lord's "day" as repeated and enlarged expression
language.detail: Tyndale notes that the term "dia" occurs repeatedly in 1:8-15 and may refer to the beginning of historical reversal, but also to the final horizon of universal judgment. Matthew Henry also reads the book as a promise of the Messiah's kingdom.
language.readingImpact: The expression should not only be read as dating, but as a theological framework that connects local crisis and universal judgment.

language.title: Retribution in proverbial language
language.detail: The notes define 1:15 by the logic of lex talionis: as you did, so will it be done with you. The image of the cup of revenge reinforces the parallelism between action and response.
language.readingImpact: This language makes the book sound like condensed moral wisdom: history snakes exactly what has been sown.

language.title: Imagtic fire, mountain and kingdom
language.detail: Obadiah is described with fire consuming Edom, mountains of Zion and Esau, and the return to Zion. The notes treat these images as an anticip of the universal realm of the Lord.
language.readingImpact: The imagery vocabulary unites destruction and hope: fire to Edom, mount to Zion, kingdom for the Lord.

timeline.title: Origin of Edom in the lineage of Esau
timeline.detail: The sources connect Edom to Esau, Jacob's brother, emphasizing an ancient rivalry that already shapes the reading of the book.
timeline.readingImpact: The conflict of Obadias gains genealogical depth: it is not only political dispute, but a rupture of historically charged kinship.

timeline.title: Period of Israeli monarchy
timeline.detail: Tyndale says that Edom existed throughout most of Israel's monarchy, approximately between 1050-856 BC, often vassal of Judah.
timeline.readingImpact: This broadens the horizon of Obadiah: the prophecy is born within centuries of unequal coexistence between the two peoples, not from an isolated event.

timeline.title: Earlier Conflicts between Edom and Israel
timeline.detail: The notes recall Edom's opposition to the exodus of Israel and other historical tensions with the house of Judah.
timeline.readingImpact: Obadiah is read in the light of accumulated hostility, which makes the accusation of 1:10-14 part of a long memory of enmity.

timeline.title: Destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC
timeline.detail: The fall of Jerusalem is presented as the decisive occasion for prophecy, with exiled Judah and Zedekiah deposed by Nebuchadnezzar.
timeline.readingImpact: This milestone situates the book in a concrete national crisis and explains the pain, indignation and urgency of judgment present in the text.

timeline.title: Possible written right after 586 BC
timeline.detail: Tyndale claims that Obadiah probably wrote shortly after the destruction of Jerusalem; Matthew Henry mentions this date as one of the main proposals, although there are those who place it before.
timeline.readingImpact: The literary and emotional context of the book becomes more comprehensible as an immediate reaction to the catastrophe, even though the exact date remains discussed.

timeline.title: Historical outcome of Edom and Idumeia
timeline.detail: Tyndale claims that Edom was probably infiltrated and supplanted by Arab kingdoms between 600-400 BC and that, in post-exile times and the New Testament, reappears as Idumeia.
timeline.readingImpact: The reading of the judgment on Edom gains a later historical reach: the nation announced in Obadiah is already in transformation when the biblical tradition progresses.

investigation: The traditional authorship is associated with the prophet Obadiah, whose name means "servant of the Lord," but the sources observe that he is known only by this prophecy.
Matthew Henry records an ancient tradition that identifies him with the administrator of Ahab's house, but rejects it as a conjecture without sufficient basis.

The sources differ only in the chronological framework: Tyndale favors post-586 BC date; Matthew Henry admits this possibility and also mentions an older date, linked to prophets such as Hosea, Joel and Amos.
There is literary/thematic dependence between Obadiah and Jeremiah 49:9, 14-16; the note suggests that Obadiah can expand other oracles on Edom.
Tyndale mentions a possible relationship with Joel 3:19 and Amos 9:12, but this is presented as a probable reading, not as absolute certainty.
The exact historical extent of Edom's participation in the fall of Jerusalem is not detailed outside Obadiah; the note itself recognizes the scarcity of specific references.

The confessional readings of the sources see Obadiah as a proclamation of the kingdom of God, and for Tyndale, as hope fulfilled in Christ; this must be noted as theological perspective of the notes, not as an independent historical conclusion.
dossier.limits: This dossier depends solely on the introductions and annexed notes of Tyndale and Matthew Henry. Therefore, there are real gaps: little direct information about verifiable historical authorship, no safe biographical detail about the prophet, and selective coverage especially of Obadiah 1. The dates presented are approximated when the source thus gives them; no chronologies were reconstructed beyond what the notes claim. There is also controversy as to the date of composition, recognized by the sources themselves. Some elements are interpretative, such as legal reading, the universal reach of the "day of the Lord" and the relationship with the Messianic kingdom; they were signaled as such not to mix inference with explicit affirmation.
